teaser.text: Williams runs the infrastructure that gets natural gas from a producer’s well to a customer who can use it. Its business is called midstream because it sits between production and final consumption, gathering, preparing, transporting, storing and marketing energy.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Williams?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA is the forecast's main operating judgment. The starting estimate is $8,400 million, the midpoint of management's 2026 guidance. The base case blends annual EBITDA rising through the project cycle, producing $8,875 million at the first date and $10,075 million at the final date. The record of growth from 2021 through 2025, the exact achievement of the 2025 midpoint and contracted projects support that path.

The bear case requires project delays or overruns while growth spending remains high. Momentum and new power projects then add less cash per share, interest and refinancing concerns rise, and the multiple contracts. The price falls to $44.52 at the first date and $33.28 at the final date, including dividends. Its probability is 25% because the funding gap is material, but contracted earnings and current guidance make a sustained downturn less likely.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Williams really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash reached $5,898 million in 2025, above net income of $2,618 million. Depreciation lowers profit without requiring a second cash payment that year, because the construction was paid for earlier. Capital spending is different: it is a current cash outflow. Williams spent $4,893 million on capital projects, leaving $1,005 million of free cash flow.

blocks.heading: How much does Williams pay per share?

paragraphs.text: At $69.22, shares carry a 27.6x trailing P/E. Their 1.2% free-cash-flow yield is below the 3.0% dividend yield. Revenue growth must convert into real free cash flow as a share of revenue. The 2025 turn in that margin came as net debt rose to $29,298 million. Williams’s own free cash flow per share was $0.82 against dividends paid of $1.99 per share.

The dividend starts at $2.10 per share after the stated 2026 increase. The base case keeps the recent roughly 5% growth pattern, reaching $2.18 and $2.40 across the forecast dates. The bear case freezes it at $2.10 because free cash flow did not cover dividends and growth capital is substantial. The bull case assumes 6% increases, reaching $2.20 and $2.44, because stronger project cash flow creates room above guidance.

blocks.heading: Does Williams’s dividend fit its cash?

paragraphs.text: Across 2021–2025, Williams generated $12,170 million of free cash flow. It paid $11,000 million in common dividends. Buybacks were only $139 million, while payments to minority owners reached $1,105 million. Together, these distributions exceeded five-year free cash flow by $74 million.

The gap became sharper in 2025. Free cash flow was $1,005 million, while common dividends were $2,442 million. Including minority distributions, Williams paid out $1,696 million more than free cash flow. Free cash flow comes after operating costs and capital spending, not after dividends and acquisitions, so expansion and shareholder payments together required financing beyond that year’s internally generated cash.

earnings.title: Williams earnings date and guidance
earnings.meta_description: Williams reports on November 2, 2026; guidance, past delivery and cash conversion are the key checks.
earnings.opening: Williams' next results are expected on November 2, 2026. Watch whether projects turn construction spending into cash.
earnings.closing: The full Williams memo also answers how its business works, who its rivals are, how management is paid, and what risks could disrupt it.

paragraphs.text: Management guides to adjusted EBITDA of $8,300–$8,500 million. EBITDA measures operating earnings before interest, taxes and depreciation; “adjusted” removes specified items. AFFO, or available funds from operations, is closer to cash, but it remains the company’s own adjusted measure. Williams expects adjusted earnings per share of $2.30–$2.40 and AFFO of $6,310–$6,440 million.

Growth capital has risen to $7,300–$7,900 million from the earlier $6,100–$6,700 million range. Maintenance capital, which keeps existing assets safe and reliable, is separately guided at $850–$950 million. The annualized dividend remains $2.10 per share, after 5.0% growth.

blocks.heading: Did Williams keep its past promise?

paragraphs.text: One promise was met: Williams forecast adjusted EBITDA of US$7.75 billion at the midpoint and reported US$7.750 billion. That supports the company’s forecasting record, although the result spans both CEOs and does not prove that every new investment will earn enough.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Williams' next release?

paragraphs.text: At the November 3, 2026 earnings call, investors should look for updates on Socrates, Atlas, construction costs and Momentum’s effect on cash generation and borrowing. Socrates’ first 200-megawatt phase entered service in July on time and within budget, but the remaining work must repeat that execution.
